paragraphs: In 2016, a Princeton professor called Johannes Haushofer published an unusual document online: a "CV of failures". Instead of listing his degrees and awards, it listed the jobs he had not got, the scholarships he had been refused and the papers that journals had rejected. To his surprise, it went viral. "This darn CV of failures has received way more attention than my entire body of academic work," he later joked.

Part of the reason it struck a chord is that we rarely see other people's failures. Social media, job applications and even conversations with friends tend to show a carefully selected version of our lives, full of successes. As a result, it is easy to believe that everyone else succeeds at the first attempt, and that our own setbacks are a sign that we are not good enough.

Psychologists who study learning tell a different story. Making mistakes, especially when we receive useful feedback afterwards, is one of the most effective ways to learn. In some experiments, people who tried to answer questions before being taught the material, and got many of them wrong, remembered more afterwards than people who simply studied the answers.

The psychologist Carol Dweck has popularised the idea of a "growth mindset": the belief that abilities can be developed through effort and good strategies, rather than being fixed. People with this mindset, she argues, are more likely to see failures as information rather than as a verdict on their worth. Later research has found the effects of mindset training to be smaller than early studies suggested, but the basic idea remains influential in schools and companies.

None of this means that failure is pleasant, or that we should celebrate every mistake. Losing a job or failing an important exam can be painful, and some failures have serious consequences. The point is rather to separate what we did from who we are, and to ask a useful question: what can I learn from this?
Perhaps that is why Haushofer's CV continues to circulate. It reminds us that behind every success story there is usually a much longer, and much less visible, list of rejections.
